__comment: NVisionX Connectors Detail — merges all 8 connector dashboards (CIFS, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, Box, SharePoint, Xberg, S3 Parquet) that previously lived as up to 24 separate files (Overview/Pipeline/Runtime x 5 V2 connectors, plus 3 standalone V1 connector dashboards) into one file, one collapsed row per connector. Each row repeats per client selected in the Clients picker (same row-repeat pattern already proven in backups-all-clients.json / scan-activity-all-clients.json). Trade-off: the old per-pod and per-query-type/datasource-id filter pickers are dropped (wildcarded to show everything) because Grafana cannot correctly cascade a chained query-type variable per repeated row instance - only non-chained custom-type pickers (the Scanner/Content 'component' split) survive, renamed per-connector to avoid collisions. namespace is hardcoded to 'default', the only namespace actually in use. 2026-09-18: built to replace dashboard sprawl per manager request for ~8-10 total dashboards, each client-selectable.

options.content:
**Connectors Detail** — one section per connector, each repeating once per client selected in the **Clients** picker (top of page). Expand a connector's row to see its full golden-signal, business-metric, and runtime detail for the selected client(s).

**Note:** this view intentionally drops the old per-pod and per-query-type filters that existed on the individual connector dashboards — Grafana can't cascade those correctly once a row repeats per client, so they're aggregated here instead. The Scanner/Content split (where a connector has one) is preserved via its own picker.

panels.title: Files Discovered (total)
panels.description: Files the scanner discovered, totalled over the selected range rather than averaged as a rate. Reads 0 when nothing ran in the window; the backlog panels tell idle from stuck.

panels.title: Items Sent (total)
panels.description: Items the scanner handed to the batch sender, totalled over the selected range. Compare against Files Discovered; the difference is in Item Loss.

panels.title: Item Loss (total)
panels.description: Files discovered minus items sent over the selected range. Should be 0. A non-zero value is broken down by cause in Items Failed.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_files_discovered_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) - (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*", outcome="sent"}[$__range])) or vector(0))

panels.title: Directories Forked (total)
panels.description: Directories published to NATS as separate work, totalled over the selected range. One per subdirectory found, so it tracks the shape of the tree rather than its file count.

panels.title: Content Fetches (total)
panels.description: Content fetch attempts, totalled over the selected range. Counts every outcome including failures, since the counter is partitioned by error_code.

panels.title: Augmenter Items (total)
panels.description: Items the augmenter processed, totalled over the selected range. All outcomes summed; the per-outcome breakdown is in the Augmenter row.

panels.title: Cost per File Discovered
panels.description: Directory-processing time per file discovered, from the scan duration total divided by files discovered over the selected range. Includes each directory's fan-out, so trees with more directories read higher.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_scan_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_files_discovered_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: ACL Cost per Item Augmented
panels.description: Average duration of one ACL query during augment, from the ACL duration total divided by items processed. One query per item; the statx and URN resolve each item also needs are not included.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_acl_query_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: Cost per Content Fetch
panels.description: Mean duration of one content fetch, from the fetch duration total divided by the fetch count. Scales with file size rather than file count.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_count{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: Items Failed (5m)
panels.description: Rate of items that never reached the batch sender, both causes summed. marshal_failed is bad data, batch_send_failed is the sender or NATS; the split is on the pipeline board.

panels.title: Dir Processing p95
panels.description: Wall-clock to process one directory: listing its entries, statx per file, ACL query when enabled, and publishing the items. Observed once per directory, so it does not measure a whole scan.

panels.title: Scanner Throughput (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Discovered = files that reached processing; sent = items that made it into a batch; failed = items that did not. Discovered equals sent plus failed by construction.

panels.title: Directory Processing — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Wall-clock to process one directory: listing its entries, statx per file, ACL query when enabled, and publishing the items. Observed once per directory, so it does not measure a whole scan.

panels.title: NATS — Scanner Backlog
panels.description: Messages waiting on the scanner durable. Scanner and augmenter share this one durable, so it blends fork and item-batch work and the two cannot be separated here. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter, so it carries no namespace or pod labels.

panels.title: NATS — In Flight (unacked)
panels.description: Delivered but not yet acked: work currently inside the pods. Also the signal KEDA's ack-capacity trigger scales on. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: NATS — Redelivered
panels.description: Messages redelivered after an ack timeout. Sustained growth with a flat items-sent rate means the connector is not draining. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter, so it carries no namespace or pod labels.

panels.title: Replicas
panels.description: Current replicas of the scanner deployment, from the HPA KEDA manages. minReplicaCount is 0, so 0 replicas with an empty queue is normal.

panels.title: Max Replicas
panels.description: Ceiling from the ScaledObject. Replicas pinned here while the backlog grows means the connector is capped, not idle.

panels.title: NATS — Backlog Slope (2m)
panels.description: Per-second growth of the backlog, clamped at 0. Verbatim the query KEDA's trend-based trigger evaluates; above 0.5 it asks for more pods.

panels.title: NATS — Scanner Consumer Backlog
panels.description: Backlog on JE_CIFS/cifs-scanner-v1 over time. Scanner and augmenter share this durable, so it blends fork and item-batch work. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter, so it carries no namespace or pod labels.

panels.title: KEDA — Replicas: current vs desired vs max
panels.description: current below desired means scaling is in progress or blocked; current pinned at max means capped. Scale-down is deliberately slow (cooldown 900s, 600s stabilization window), so a flat line for ten minutes after a burst is configuration, not a stuck HPA.

panels.title: KEDA — ack-capacity signal vs threshold
panels.description: KEDA's ack-capacity trigger: replicas = ceil(ack_pending / 1000). The red line is that threshold; crossing it is what asks for another pod.

panels.title: KEDA — trend-based signal vs threshold
panels.description: KEDA's trend-based trigger: slope of the backlog over 2m, clamped at 0 so only growth counts. Threshold 0.5, activation 0.1. The pipeline-full trigger is not rendered in dev (capacity is unset), so this plus ack-capacity and pending-wakeup is the whole scaling story.

panels.title: Augmenter Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Terminal outcome per item the augmenter touched. outcome="missing" is also counted by items_skipped_not_found_total for the same event, so never sum the two.

panels.title: Augmenter ACL Query Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
Pods Up
panels.description: Content pods scale 0↔N with KEDA — 0 pods with an empty queue is normal.

panels.title: Errors (5m)
panels.description: Number of content fetch requests that failed in the last 5 minutes. Counter increase on cifs_content_fetch_total{success="false"}.

panels.title: Upload Throughput
panels.description: Bytes per second confirmed by the content transfer service (rate over cifs_content_uploaded_bytes_total).

panels.title: Mount Acquire p95 (5m)
panels.description: p95 of successful mount acquires on the content pod. Failed acquires are tracked separately (cifs_content_mount_acquire_failure_duration_seconds).

panels.title: Content Fetches by error_code (rate, 5m)
panels.description: error_code="NONE" is the success path; NAK_* codes are infra-level failures.

panels.title: Content Requests In-Flight
panels.description: Requests currently inside the handler — content-mode saturation signal (the counterpart of the scanner's worker_busy). Authoritative backlog (num_pending) lives on the NATS server.

panels.title: NATS — Content Consumer Redelivery
panels.description: nats_consumer_num_redelivered for the content durable (content-fetch-cifs). Rising = fetch requests failing and being retried; sustained growth toward MaxDeliver=3 means messages are about to be dropped as poison. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: KEDA — Content Replicas: current vs desired vs max
panels.description: The content deployment scales independently of the scanner, off its own ScaledObject watching CONTENT_FETCH/content-fetch-cifs.

panels.title: KEDA — Content Trigger Signals
panels.description: Signals behind the content ScaledObject. The consumer_name regex covers both the batch durable and the interactive one used by See Content, which has its own interactive-wakeup trigger. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: Files Gone (5m)
panels.description: Files gone from the share when the augmenter or the content fetcher returned for them, counted over the last 5 minutes. Decays as the window slides, so it shows current activity rather than a run total. The content half also fires for symlinks and other non-regular files.

targets.expr: (sum(increase(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*", outcome="missing"}[5m])) or vector(0)) + (sum(increase(cifs_content_fetch_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*", error_code="FETCH_ERROR_NOT_FOUND"}[5m])) or vector(0))

panels.title: Files Gone % (augment)
panels.description: Share of augmented items whose file was already gone, over the selected range. Augment only: content fetches one file per request and has no comparable denominator.

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*", outcome="missing"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1))

panels.title: Files Gone by stage (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Missing files split by the stage that found them missing; augment and content fetch are different moments and are diagnosed differently. The content series counts FETCH_ERROR_NOT_FOUND, which also fires for non-regular files.

panels.title: Scanner Items by Outcome (rate)
panels.description: Terminal outcome per file the scanner processed, plotted against the discovery rate. The outcomes sum to discovered; marshal_failed is bad data, batch_send_failed is the sender or NATS.

panels.title: Directories Forked vs Local (rate)
panels.description: forked = directories fanned out to the work channel; local = directories walked inline on the local stack.

panels.title: Entries per Directory — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Entries found in one directory, observed once per directory. Files and subdirectories are both counted, so it reads higher than the directory's file count.

panels.title: Discovery → Sent Conversion
panels.description: Share of discovered files that made it into a batch. Below 1 means items are dropped between discovery and send. Reads as a gap while nothing is being discovered.

panels.title: Item Loss (discovered − sent)
panels.description: Absolute loss rate. Sustained above zero means items are not reaching the batch sender; the outcome panel says which of the two causes.

panels.title: File Operation Duration p95 by operation
Worker Pool — busy / pool size / channel depth
Scanner ACL Query Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
Work Channel Wait p95 — submit vs collect
Directory Processing — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Wall-clock to process one directory: listing its entries, statx per file, ACL query when enabled, and publishing the items. Observed once per directory, so it does not measure a whole scan.

panels.title: Augmenter Items by Outcome (rate, stacked)
panels.description: All 12 outcomes: success, missing, stat_failed, acl_error, acl_skipped, build_failed, send_failed, invalid_urn, mount_failed, unc_mismatch, cancelled_stat, cancelled_acl.

panels.title: Augmenter Mount Acquire p95 — success vs failure
panels.description: Success and failure acquires are separate histograms so a hung mount.cifs (~120s) does not poison the success p95.

panels.title: Augmenter Publish Blocked — p99
panels.description: Time spent blocked publishing augmented items downstream. Sustained growth means backpressure from the stream.

panels.title: Augmenter ACL Query Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
Content Fetches by error_code (rate, stacked)
panels.description: error_code="NONE" is the success path; NAK_* codes are infra-level failures.

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: End-to-end duration per successful fetch request. The histogram intentionally carries only the success label, so percentiles are computed over success="true".

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.title: Content Fetch Bytes — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Size of files streamed successfully (buckets 1KiB×4^10). Useful for sizing impact of large-payload streaming and spotting outliers.

panels.title: Uploaded Bytes (rate)
panels.description: Bytes per second confirmed by the content transfer service.

panels.title: Content Mount Acquire p95 — success vs failure
panels.description: Success and failure acquires are separate histograms so a hung mount.cifs (~120s) does not poison the success p95.

panels.title: Fetch Errors by error_code (increase, 1h)
panels.description: Triage table: non-NONE error codes over the last hour. NAK_* codes are infra-level failures (NATS NAK path).

panels.title: Content Upload Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: CIFS-read + gRPC-upload leg only (the uploadFile call), isolated from mount-acquire and end-to-end so a slow content-service is distinguishable from a slow CIFS read. Success-labelled like fetch duration.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_upload_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_upload_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(cifs_content_upload_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.title: Content Requests In-Flight
panels.description: Saturation signal — requests currently inside the handler (Inc on entry, Dec on exit), the content-mode counterpart of the scanner's worker_busy. Sustained pinning at peak means capacity-bound; the authoritative backlog (num_pending) lives on the NATS server.

panels.title: NATS — Content Consumer Redelivery
panels.description: Redeliveries on the content durable. Rising means fetch requests are failing and being retried; sustained growth toward MaxDeliver=3 means messages are about to be dropped as poison. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter, so it carries no namespace or pod labels.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, datasource_id) (rate(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, datasource_id) (rate(cifs_content_upload_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.title: Content Latency per MiB (interim)
panels.description: Read and upload time per MiB streamed, success path only. Flat while fetch duration climbs means the cost is per request, not per byte. An average of averages: the byte and duration histograms are separate series, so many small files and one large file land on the same point.

panels.title: Average Bytes per Fetch
panels.description: Mean size of what content is moving. Pair it with the panel on the left: a latency jump with a flat mean size is a slowdown, one that tracks mean size is just bigger files.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, pod) (rate(go_gc_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"${cifs_component}", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])))

panels.title: Connections (Open)
panels.description: Open MySQL connections summed across every active scanner pool. Pools are per-datasource and created/evicted at runtime, so this is a scrape-time aggregate, not a fixed ceiling.

panels.title: ScanStart In Flight
panels.description: ScanStart handler invocations currently doing database discovery and DatabaseFork fan-out. The per-table leaf work that runs after fan-out is counted separately (see Tables In Flight on the pipeline dashboard).

panels.title: Items Sent (5m)
panels.description: Items successfully submitted through ItemBatchSender.UpsertItem, per second.

panels.title: Scan p95 (5m)
panels.description: p95 of the ScanStart discovery + fan-out phase. Histogram ladder is 0.5s to ~1024s, so this measures how long it takes to enumerate databases and hand out work — not how long a whole scan takes end to end.

panels.title: Error Rate (5m)
panels.description: Query failures against the source database, per second: database_errors_total + table_errors_total. Skipped tables and connector bugs are counted apart — see the Silent-Failure Signals row.

panels.title: Table Panics (5m)
panels.description: Leaf-worker tasks that panicked. Always a connector bug, never a source-database fault — counted apart from table_errors_total so a panic on an unexpected column shape doesn't read as the customer's MySQL refusing a query. Any non-zero value is worth acting on.

panels.title: Inline Fallback (5m)
panels.description: Tables the worker pool refused, run inline on the NATS consumer goroutine instead of being dropped. The pool only refuses after Shutdown, so non-zero means a scan was still fanning out while the process was tearing down — accounting stays exact, but the rest of that database serialises onto one goroutine.

panels.title: No Visible Columns (5m)
panels.description: Tables skipped because INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS returned no rows — a missing column-level GRANT, or a table dropped mid-scan. The query succeeded, so this is not a query failure. Alert on a sustained rate, not on any non-zero value.

panels.title: Error Reports Dropped (5m)
panels.description: Structured errors that never reached the observer, across all reasons (buffer_full, after_close, publish_failed). Non-zero means the job record is showing a truncated view of the scan's failures. Break down by reason on the pipeline dashboard.

panels.title: Connections (Open)
panels.description: Open MySQL connections summed across active content-fetch pools. A climb that does not come back down alongside a non-zero Conn Discard failure is the pool-exhaustion signature described on that panel.

panels.title: Fetch In Flight
panels.description: Content fetch requests currently being processed.

panels.title: Fetch p95 (5m)
panels.description: p95 end-to-end fetch latency for successful requests only: handler entry (URN parse, datasource resolve, conn acquire) through stream completion and reply publish. Errors are filtered out so a fast failure doesn't flatter the number.

panels.title: Errors (5m)
panels.description: Content requests that errored in the last 5 minutes — counter increase on mysql_content_requests_total{outcome="error"}.

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
Producer Panics (5m)
panels.description: Streaming producers that panicked and were recovered. Always a connector bug: the requester is told INTERNAL/retryable and the message is redelivered, so nothing in the request's own outcome says this connector crashed.

panels.title: Byte Mismatch (5m)
panels.description: Uploads whose stored size disagreed with the sampled/streamed byte count. The handler NAKs without replying, so a single count is a transient that a redelivery repaired; a sustained rate means the same URN fails verification every attempt, and once MaxDeliver is spent the object proven wrong stays under that URN with no reply ever sent.

panels.title: Conn Discard Failures (5m)
panels.description: Abandoned result sets whose connection could NOT be discarded (outcome != "discarded"). The discard is the only defence against the driver's uncancellable drain of the rest of a multi-GB column — a drain that ignores the query deadline and SIGTERM while holding a pool connection and a worker slot. Non-zero means the byte budget stops bounding what crosses the wire, and the symptom surfaces as pool exhaustion rather than an error.

panels.title: Sample Re-draws (5m)
panels.description: Content fetches whose first random draw fell under MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_MIN_ROWS and were re-drawn at a higher percent, all outcomes summed. Each re-draw is an extra table scan, so a sustained rate means MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_PERCENT is set too low for the tables being classified — raise the percent, not the floor. Break down by outcome on the pipeline dashboard: "failed" is a different problem and points at the query timeout and the source database.

panels.title: Tables & Columns Discovered (rate)
panels.description: Tables successfully scanned and columns retrieved, per second. Tables that failed or were skipped are not in these counters — see the Errors & Silent Failures row.

panels.title: Items & Batches Sent (rate)
panels.description: items/s is the connector's own mysql_scanner_items_sent_total. The other two come from the shared ItemBatchSender in pipeline-lib-go and carry no connector prefix, so they are filtered by job — batches/s is how often the batch is flushed to JobEngine.

panels.title: Scan Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: ScanStart database discovery + fan-out phase, on a 0.5s–1024s ladder. This runs on the single pod that received the ScanStart message; the leaf work it hands out is not included.

panels.title: Scanner Errors (rate)
panels.description: Query failures against the source database. These are the only two counters that mean "MySQL refused something" — everything on the next two panels is deliberately kept out of them.

panels.title: Skips & Connector Bugs (count, 5m)
panels.description: Three failure modes counted apart from table_errors_total because none of them is the source database's fault. no visible columns — INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS returned nothing (missing column-level GRANT, or a table dropped mid-scan); alert on a sustained rate, not any non-zero value. inline fallback — the worker pool refused a table after Shutdown and the scanner ran it on the consumer goroutine, serialising the rest of that database. table panics — always a connector bug, any non-zero value is worth acting on.

panels.title: Error Reporter Drops by Reason (count, 5m)
panels.description: Structured errors that never reached the observer, so the job record is showing a truncated view of the scan's failures. buffer_full — the buffered channel saturated. after_close — PublishError called after Close. publish_failed — the observer refused or could not be reached; this is the remote failure mode, and without it an unreachable observer used to lose every ItemError while the drop counter stayed at zero. close timeouts counts one abandonment of an unknown number of reports rather than individual errors, which is why it is a separate series: reaching it means publishLoop was parked inside a single publish for the whole flush budget, so check the control plane's health, not the scan.

panels.title: Error Reporter — Abandoned Flushes (live)
panels.description: Abandoned error-reporter flushes whose background goroutine is still parked in a publish — a live count on this pod, not a rate. Its sibling on the panel to the left counts how many times an abandonment has happened since the pod started; this one is how many are outstanding right now, which is the number that says whether the pod is still healthy. The two differ because an ErrorReporter is built and closed per message (one per ScanStart, one per DatabaseFork): an abandoned flush leaves a goroutine plus its 100-slot buffer behind, and the error that Close's caller returns NAKs the message, so redelivery supplies another fork that does it again. It unwinds on its own — each goroutine exits as soon as its publish returns — so a value that climbs and stays up is a control plane that is not answering, not a leak the connector can close from the inside. On the pinned pipeline-lib-go that publish resolves the job's step through GetJobSettings on a context with no deadline, which is why there is nothing bounding it below the reporter's 5s flush budget. Sustained above zero is alert-worthy; check the control plane, not the scan.

panels.title: Query Duration Heatmap
panels.description: Scanner-path SQL latency distribution, on a 10ms–20s ladder.

panels.title: Query p95 by query_type
panels.description: query_type is list_tables (INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES per database) or query_columns (INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS per table). A list_tables p95 climbing alone points at a database with a very wide table count; query_columns climbing points at the tables themselves.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, query_type) (rate(mysql_scanner_query_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", query_type=~".*"}[5m])))

panels.title: Scanner Connections by Type
panels.description: Aggregated across every active scanner pool at scrape time. in-use pinned at open with idle at zero is the pool running at its ceiling.

panels.title: Scanner — In Flight
panels.description: scanstart is the discovery + fan-out phase on the pod that received ScanStart. tables (leaf pool) is the per-table work the fan-out handed to the worker pool — the two are counted separately on purpose, so a busy leaf pool does not look like a stuck ScanStart.

panels.title: Query Rate by query_type
panels.description: Observation count on the query-duration histogram — how many scanner-path queries are actually being issued, split by kind.

panels.title: Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99 by outcome
panels.description: End-to-end request latency, split by outcome so a fast failure does not flatter the success distribution: handler entry (URN parse, datasource resolve, conn acquire) through stream completion and reply publish.

panels.title: Stream Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: The streaming pipeline only — from the producer goroutine pulling its first row out of MySQL until UploadFrom returns. Excludes handler setup. Query and upload run concurrently, so this reflects whichever leg is slower at any moment; the gap between this and Fetch Duration is setup cost.

panels.title: Stream Bytes — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Bytes per successful fetch, taken from UploadResponse.Size — the count the content transfer service actually stored, not Info.Size, which this connector leaves at 0 because a sample's length is unknown until the last row streams. Ladder runs 1KiB to 4GiB.

panels.title: Stream Throughput (bytes/s)
panels.description: Sum of stored bytes per second across successful fetches.

panels.title: Stream Rows — Rate (rows/s)
panels.description: Sampled rows written per second across successful fetches.

panels.title: Stream Rows — Avg per Fetch
panels.description: Average sampled rows per successful fetch (sum / count over the window). Compare against MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_MIN_ROWS and MAX_ROWS: sitting at the ceiling means the sampler is being capped, sitting at the floor means it is being rescued by re-draws.

panels.title: Sample Re-draws by Outcome (count, 5m)
panels.description: Fetches whose first draw fell under MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_MIN_ROWS and were re-drawn at a higher percent. recovered — a later draw reached the floor. short — every draw stayed under it, and since the final draw runs at 100% that means the column genuinely holds fewer non-NULL values than the floor, not a sampling miss. failed — a draw errored before finishing, so its row count says nothing about the column; kept separate so a broken query is not read as a small column. A fourth case carries no label and appears in none of these: a draw torn down because the upload died. During a content-service outage the three series therefore do not sum to the number of fetches that re-drew. Sustained recovered/short means raise MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_PERCENT, not the floor — each re-draw is an extra table scan. Sustained failed is a different problem: look at the query timeout and the source database.

panels.title: Sample Percent Used
panels.description: The percent the streamed draw actually ran at. It equals MYSQL_CONTENT_SAMPLE_PERCENT whenever the first draw was kept, so drift above the configured value is the signal that the row floor is doing the work instead of the percent.

panels.title: Conn Discard by Outcome (count, 5m)
panels.description: Abandoned result sets whose driver connection was thrown away rather than drained. discarded — the connection was closed so the driver skips its post-finish drain; the intended path. unsupported — the Querier exposed no raw connection, so nothing could be closed and the DSN's ReadTimeout is the only bound left on the drain. close_error — the raw-connection callback or the Close itself failed, so the drain very likely still happened. Anything other than discarded is worth alerting on: the byte budget stops bounding what crosses the wire, and the symptom is pool exhaustion rather than an error anyone would connect back to sampling.

panels.title: Content Bugs (count, 5m)
panels.description: producer panics — a streaming producer panicked and was recovered; the requester is told INTERNAL/retryable and the message is redelivered, so nothing in the request's own outcome says this connector crashed. byte mismatch — the stored size disagreed with what was sampled and streamed; the handler NAKs without replying, so one count is a transient a redelivery repaired, while a repeating one means the same URN fails verification every attempt and once MaxDeliver is spent the object proven wrong stays under that URN with no reply ever sent.

panels.title: Content Connections (Open) by Pod
panels.description: Per-pod so one replica leaking connections stands out from the aggregate.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: cAdvisor series, so it is selected by pod name rather than by job — the Component variable does not filter this panel.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description: cAdvisor series, so it is selected by pod name rather than by job — the Component variable does not filter this panel. This is the number the OOM killer watches, not process RSS.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: A count that climbs and never comes back down across scans is the leak signature — the leaf worker pool and the content streaming producers are the two places goroutines are spawned per unit of work.

panels.title: GC Pause (max / p75)
panels.description: go_gc_duration_seconds is a SUMMARY, not a histogram — there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile against it returns nothing. These are the pre-computed quantiles the Go collector exports; the available ones are 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1, so there is no p99 to plot. The label is matched with =~ because client_golang formats these values as "0.0"/"1.0" here while older versions emit "0"/"1" — an exact quantile="1" silently returns nothing.

panels.title: GC Cycles (rate)
panels.description: Completed GC cycles per second, from the summary's observation count. A rate that climbs alongside flat heap in-use means allocation churn rather than growth.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Every pooled MySQL connection is a socket, so an open count converging on max is how connection-pool exhaustion presents at the process level.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Scanner pods only — the trailing anchor on the job matcher keeps the -content pods out.

panels.title: Fan-out p95 (5m)
panels.description: The scanner fan-out only: connect, list databases, publish the per-database work items. Not an end-to-end scan duration — the per-schema and per-table work runs in other handler invocations, on other pods, and is not timed today. Buckets are ExponentialBuckets(0.05, 2, 12) — 50ms to ~102s.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(postgresql_connector_database_errors_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(postgresql_connector_table_errors_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(postgresql_connector_columns_failed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])) or vector(0))

panels.title: Fetch p95 (5m)
panels.description: Success path only. ContentFetchDuration is labelled by success, and failures time out on a completely different scale, so folding them in would distort the percentile.

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Success path only, for the same reason as the Fetch p95 stat.

panels.title: Databases & Schemas Discovered (rate)
panels.description: The two fan-out stages: pg_database enumeration on the ScanStart handler, then pg_namespace enumeration on each DatabaseFork. Schemas rising with databases flat is normal mid-scan — the forks are being worked through.

panels.title: Tables & Columns Discovered (rate)
panels.description: Tables successfully scanned and columns retrieved from pg_catalog. Columns are added per table in the bulk path and per column list in the fallback path, so the ratio between the two lines tracks average table width.

panels.title: Items Sent (rate)
panels.description: Items accepted by ItemBatchSender.UpsertItem, against batches actually published to NATS. UpsertItem only appends to the current batch, so items/s counts items queued; batches/s is incremented after a successful publish. A sustained items/s with batches/s flat is a failing Flush() — items counted but never published. connector_batches_sent_total comes from pipeline-lib-go and is not connector-prefixed, so it is scoped by job here; every connector writes to the same series.

panels.title: Fan-out Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: The ScanStart discovery + fan-out phase only: connect, list databases, publish the DatabaseFork work items. It is not an end-to-end scan duration — the per-schema and per-table work runs in separate handler invocations, on other pods, and is not timed anywhere today.

panels.title: Scanner Errors (rate)
panels.description: Four different failure shapes, deliberately kept apart. database_errors_total: seven increment sites that do not all mean the same thing. Three abort the run outright (maintenance-pool connect, connection verify, list-databases); one takes down a single database's branch (list-schemas); three more fire on per-database pool acquisition, and of those, one falls back to table mode and keeps scanning rather than returning. So a non-zero line here is not proof the scan stopped — read it against Items Sent before treating it as fatal. table_errors_total: a table query failed, or a bulk schema query took a whole schema down. columns_failed_total: individual columns were dropped while the scan otherwise succeeded (per-column anypb/URN/upsert failures) — a non-zero line here with a flat items/s is silent data loss. permissions_failed_total: a table's grants could not be read, so its items shipped with empty permissions — the data is published but degraded, which is why it is not folded into the Error Rate stat.

panels.title: Tables In Flight vs Pool Size
panels.description: Occupancy of the per-pod table worker pool, against its configured size. The pool is per-pod (POSTGRESQL_POOL_WORKERS, 10 in the Helm values), so the series is broken out by pod rather than summed — a sum across pods would sit above the limit line and mean nothing. A pod pegged at the line is the back-pressure signal: tables are waiting on workers, not on PostgreSQL. Only table mode fills the pool; bulk mode walks a schema's tables sequentially and tops out at 1. The limit line is hard-coded from the Helm default and does not follow an override.

panels.title: Query Duration Heatmap
panels.description: Scan-path SQL latency distribution across the selected query types, on a 50ms-to-~102s ladder.

panels.title: Query p95 by query_type
panels.description: query_type values are the eight labelled call sites: list_databases and list_schemas (enumeration), count_schema_columns (auto mode's scan-mode decision, once per schema), tables_in_schema, bulk_tables and bulk_columns (the batched crawl path), list_columns (the per-table fallback), and table_permissions — which runs once per table and is normally the dominant query in a scan. A rising list_columns share means the bulk path is falling back more often. This panel also doubles as the scan-mode signal: bulk_tables/bulk_columns traffic means auto chose bulk for that schema, tables_in_schema/list_columns means it chose table mode.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, query_type) (rate(postgresql_connector_query_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", query_type=~".*"}[5m])))

panels.title: Query Rate by query_type
panels.description: Observations per second per call site, from the histogram's _count series. This is how many queries the connector is issuing, as opposed to how long they take. Expect table_permissions to dominate — it is one query per table — and expect the bulk_* pair to trade off against tables_in_schema/list_columns as auto mode picks a path per schema.

panels.title: Content Requests by Outcome (rate)
panels.description: success is a string label, "true" or "false"; error_code is "NONE" on success. Grouping by both keeps the successful and failed paths on the same axis.

panels.title: Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99 by outcome
panels.description: Split by success because a failure's latency measures how fast the handler gave up, not how fast it did the work. A p95 that improves while the error rate climbs is the failure path getting faster, not the fetch path.

panels.title: Content Errors by error_code (count, 5m)
panels.description: The distinction that matters here is transport versus reply. NAK_UNMARSHAL, NAK_PROCESSING, NAK_MARSHAL_COMPLETED and NAK_PUBLISH_COMPLETED mean the message was NAKed and will be redelivered with no reply sent — a requester waiting on that reply sees a timeout, not an error. The FETCH_ERROR_* codes were answered. Raised by the handler before the query: INVALID_URN, CREDENTIAL_FAILURE, TOO_LARGE and CACHE_WRITE_FAILED. Classified from the driver error: TIMEOUT and READ_ERROR (retryable), CONNECTION_FAILED (SQLSTATE class 08, retryable), NOT_FOUND (42P01/42703), PERMISSION_DENIED (42501), and INTERNAL as the catch-all. PERMISSION_DENIED is the one to watch — it means the content role lost a grant the scanner still has, so items keep shipping while their content never resolves. UNSPECIFIED should never appear; if it does, a nil error reached the classifier.

panels.title: Fetches per Pod (rate)
panels.description: Per-pod content fetch rate. A single pod carrying the whole load while others sit idle points at the consumer's work distribution rather than at the connector.

panels.title: Fetch Success Ratio
panels.description: Successful fetches as a fraction of all fetches over 5 minutes. With no traffic both sides of the division are zero, so the panel draws a gap rather than a value — it never renders 1 out of thin air. A flat 1 is the opposite reading: every fetch in the window succeeded. Pair it with Fetches per Pod to tell "no failures" apart from "no work".

panels.title: Document Size — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Bytes per content document produced, including what is written to the raw-content-cache. Ladder runs 1KiB to 256MiB (ExponentialBuckets(1024, 4, 10)), so a percentile sitting on the top boundary means the tail is in +Inf and its real size is unknown.

panels.title: Sample Rows per Document — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Rows serialised into each sampled document, on a 10-to-~20k ladder. Read it against Document Size: rows flat while bytes climb means wider rows, not more of them.

panels.title: Cache Write Throughput (bytes/s)
panels.description: Bytes per second this connector pushes into the raw-content-cache, from the cumulative counter. Only the success path adds to it, so it should track the success line on Content Requests by Outcome.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: cAdvisor series carry no job label, so this is selected by pod name rather than by job — which means it covers both components and deliberately ignores the Component and Pod pickers. That is the point: it keeps reporting pods that have already churned out of the scrape target list, so container history survives a scale-to-zero. Content pods are identifiable by the -content segment in the series name.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description: cAdvisor series carry no job label, so this is selected by pod name rather than by job — which means it covers both components and deliberately ignores the Component and Pod pickers. That is the point: it keeps reporting pods that have already churned out of the scrape target list, so container history survives a scale-to-zero. Content pods are identifiable by the -content segment in the series name. This is the number the OOM killer watches, not process RSS.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: A count that climbs and never comes back down across scans is the leak signature — the schema/table fan-out workers and the content fetch handlers are where goroutines are spawned per unit of work.

panels.title: GC Pause (max / p75)
panels.description: go_gc_duration_seconds is a SUMMARY, not a histogram — there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile against it returns nothing. These are the pre-computed quantiles the Go collector exports; the available ones are 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1, so there is no p99 to plot. The label is matched with =~ because client_golang formats these values as "0.0"/"1.0" here while older versions emit "0"/"1" — an exact quantile="1" silently returns nothing.

panels.title: GC Cycles (rate)
panels.description: Completed GC cycles per second, from the summary's observation count. A rate that climbs alongside flat heap in-use means allocation churn rather than growth.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Every pooled PostgreSQL connection is a socket, so an open count converging on max is how connection-pool exhaustion presents at the process level. The connector exports no pool gauges of its own, which makes this the closest available proxy.

panels.title: ScanStart In Flight
panels.description: Number of ScanStart handler invocations currently executing the prescan + fanout phase. Per-database / per-schema worker activity that runs after fanout is not counted here.

panels.title: Errors (5m)
panels.description: Number of content requests that errored in the last 5 minutes. Counter increase on snowflake_content_requests_total{outcome="error"}.

panels.title: Fetch In Flight
panels.description: Number of content fetch requests currently being processed.

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, query_type) (rate(snowflake_scanner_query_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", query_type=~".*"}[5m])))

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99 by outcome
Content Stream Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Wall-clock duration of the streaming pipeline (Snowflake row pull + UploadFrom). The two legs run concurrently through an io.Pipe, so this reflects the slower of the two at any moment. Replaces the old separate Query Duration and Upload Duration metrics, which can't be measured independently in the streaming architecture.

panels.title: Content Stream Bytes — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Bytes streamed per successful content fetch (Info.Size echoed back by the content transfer service). Useful for sizing impact of large-payload streaming and spotting outliers.

panels.title: Content Stream Rows — Rate (rows/s)
panels.description: Total rows streamed per second across successful content fetches.

panels.title: Content Stream Rows — Avg per Fetch
panels.description: Average rows streamed per successful content fetch (sum / count over a 5-minute window).

panels.title: Sample Verify-Empty by Outcome (count, 5m)
panels.description: Count of times the verify-at-100% branch fired during content sampling. outcome="recovered" means phase-1 SAMPLE SYSTEM returned zero rows on a non-empty table and the re-run rescued data — sustained > 0 means SamplePercent is too low for the row distribution. outcome="empty" means the re-run also returned nothing — table is genuinely empty, no action needed. Replaces the old sample_fallback_total metric.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, pod) (rate(go_gc_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"${snowflake_component}", namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[5m])))

panels.title: Files Discovered (total)
panels.description: File entries seen in folder listings, before any filtering. The funnel's denominator.

panels.title: Items Sent (total)
panels.description: Files the scanner handed to the item sender. The only success path out of the scan.

panels.title: Item Loss (total)

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_files_discovered_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) - (sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0))

panels.description: Discovered minus every terminal outcome. Should be zero: a non-zero value means an exit path in processFolder is uninstrumented, not that files were lost.

panels.title: Users Enumerated (total)
panels.description: Enterprise users listed at the start of a full scan. In Box the unit of fan-out is the user, so this is the real denominator of a scan.

panels.title: Folders Forked (total)
panels.description: Subfolders published to NATS as box.folder. Every subfolder becomes its own message, so this is the number of traversal units the scan created — and it is NOT proportional to files: a deep tree of empty folders still produces messages here.

panels.title: Content Fetches (total)
panels.description: ContentFetchRequest deliveries resolved by the content pods, success and failure together.

panels.title: Users Enumerated
panels.description: GET /users, paged. The denominator.

panels.title: Users Forked

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_users_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) - (sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_users_skipped_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0))

panels.description: Enumerated minus skipped: the users a box.fork was actually published for.

panels.title: Users Skipped
panels.description: Users whose content was not scanned at all, any reason. Counted once per user — the per-folder TOS path is deliberately excluded, since one TOS-blocked person has thousands of folders and would read as thousands of skipped users.

panels.title: Skip Rate

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_users_skipped_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(box_scanner_users_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1))

panels.description: Share of the enterprise whose content this scan did not cover.

panels.title: Users Skipped by Reason (total in window)
panels.description: All six reasons are exported at 0 even when nobody is skipped (InitUserSkipReasons), so an empty stack means the scan ran clean rather than that the series is missing. Only traverse_failed is a connector failure; permission_denied is broken config, and the other four are expected absence.

panels.title: User Fan-out over time (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Only legible under sustained load. With a burst that finishes inside a scrape interval both lines read 0 — use the stats above for that case.

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Zero is the normal state, not an outage: minReplicaCount is 0 and the cooldown is 900s.

panels.title: Items Failed (5m)
panels.description: Total items the scanner discovered but could not deliver: build_failed and upsert_failed added together. This is the headline loss count. For WHICH of the two it was, see 'Scanner Items by Outcome' — build_failed is bad data, upsert_failed is the sender or NATS.

panels.title: Folder p95
panels.description: One BoxFolderWork message: a single folder listing plus its publishes and upserts. This is the connector's real unit of work, and the one that makes cost predictable.

panels.title: Folder Work In-Flight
panels.description: Folder handlers running right now across the selected pods. BoxFork and BoxFolderWork both count — both process a folder.

panels.title: User Slots Held
panels.description: Cross-pod per-user admission slots held. Read against the deferral counter in the API row: slots at the cap with deferrals rising means BOX_USER_MAX_CONCURRENCY is what binds.

panels.title: Scanner Throughput (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Three near-parallel lines; the question is the gap between them. The pipeline board graphs that difference explicitly, which is the only way funnel loss is actually visible.

panels.title: Scanner Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: skipped_inactive is the scanner's half of Files Gone: the file was already in Box's trash when we listed its parent. A different moment from the incremental path's deleted outcome — see the Files Gone row, and do not add them.

panels.title: Folder Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: One BoxFolderWork message: one folder listing plus the publishes and upserts it produces. This is the connector's real unit of work — multiply its mean by a folder count to estimate a larger tenant.

panels.title: Folders by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Every subfolder is forked as its own message. skipped_collab is the owner filter: a folder owned by another user, left for that user's own fork so it is enumerated exactly once.

panels.title: Saturation — in-flight, slots, contention
panels.description: Where the scanner throttles itself. Box rate-limits per impersonated user, so the connector holds a fixed number of slots per user shared across every pod. A folder that finds no free slot waits, then is RE-PUBLISHED with its delivery count reset — 'requeues' is that path and is the normal sign of contention. 'deferrals' is the fallback once a folder exhausts BOX_USER_SLOT_MAX_REQUEUE: it NAKs, spends a delivery, and is the last step before the SDK discards the folder and its whole subtree. Requeues climbing with deferrals at zero is healthy; deferrals above zero is not.

panels.title: Scan Durations — three different units
panels.description: Three genuinely different measurements, plotted together for scale only — they are not comparable. fan-out is authenticate plus paged GET /users plus publishing one box.fork per user, and EXCLUDES the traversal. incremental is a whole run including its inline augment. root_folder is one BoxFork: a user's root level only, not their tree. 'How long did the scan take end to end' is not answerable from the connector at all — a scan is a fan-out of messages with no owner.

panels.title: NATS — Redelivered
panels.description: A connector that fails and retries in a loop shows up here and nowhere else.

panels.title: Max Replicas
panels.description: The KEDA ceiling as the HPA reports it. The value comes from the chart (autoscaling.maxReplicas) and differs per environment, so read it off the panel rather than assuming one. Desired-equals-max is not by itself a sign of trouble — read it together with the backlog: at a low ceiling it is reached routinely.

panels.title: NATS — Backlog Slope (2m)
panels.description: The trend-based trigger's own signal: messages per second the backlog is growing by.

panels.title: NATS — Scanner Consumer Backlog
panels.description: Stream JE_BOX, durable box-scanner-v1. Sustained ack_pending with items_sent at zero is the signature of a stuck connector.

panels.title: KEDA — Replicas: current vs desired vs max
panels.description: cooldownPeriod 900s and scaleDown stabilizationWindowSeconds 600s. 'It scaled ten minutes ago and is still the same' is config, not a bug.

panels.title: KEDA — ack-capacity signal vs threshold
panels.description: replicas = ceil(ack_pending / threshold), with the threshold set by the ScaledObject. The red line is that threshold as configured in this environment; crossing it is what asks for another pod.

panels.title: KEDA — trend-based signal vs threshold
panels.description: Threshold 0.5, activation 0.1. Positive slope means the backlog is growing.

panels.title: KEDA — pending-wakeup signal vs threshold
panels.description: The trigger that wakes the pod from zero: its activation threshold is 0, so a single pending message is enough. The red line is the scale threshold as configured here. The fourth trigger, pipeline-full, is NOT rendered in dev — pipelineFull.capacity is empty in the chart and the environment does not override it — so it is deliberately absent rather than drawn as a flat panel.

panels.title: API Calls (5m)
panels.description: HTTP attempts, not logical calls: doJSON retries up to BOX_MAX_RETRIES, so one GetFile can be four requests. Calls rising faster than items means we are retrying.

panels.title: Limiter Wait p95
panels.description: The LEADING saturation signal: time spent waiting on our own token bucket before a request goes out. Lowering BOX_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SEC must move this first — if it does not, the signal is not wired.

panels.title: 429s (5m)
panels.description: The LAGGING half: Box has already refused us. Known blind spot — only doJSON counts here, so a 429 on the content download path (GetFileContent, probeGet) is invisible on this series today.

panels.title: Slot Deferrals (5m)
panels.description: Folders that exhausted BOX_USER_SLOT_MAX_REQUEUE and fell back to a NAK. Each one spends a delivery, and past JOBENGINE_MAX_DELIVER the SDK discards the folder AND its subtree. Anything above zero means the requeue bound is too low for this tenant.

panels.title: API Calls by Endpoint (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Ten fixed templates, passed in by each client method rather than parsed off the URL. folder_items should dominate during a scan. The four /events values are kept apart on purpose: the cursor read is one or two pages, the admin-log backfill runs up to 200 pages per refresh, and the per-user pull runs up to 50 pages FOR EVERY USER — collapsing them would hide the one that can run away.

panels.title: API Calls by Status (rate, 5m)
panels.description: transport_error is a request that never got a response — connection reset, timeout, DNS. Deliberately distinct from any HTTP code, so 'Box refused us' and 'we never reached Box' are not the same bucket.

panels.title: Saturation — leading vs lagging
panels.description: Read left to right in time: contention shows up before Box complains. Requeues rise first (folders cannot get a slot), then limiter wait (the client throttling itself), and 429s last — by then Box is already refusing. Deferrals sit between requeues and loss: they only appear once folders exhaust the requeue bound.

panels.title: API Call Duration p95 by Endpoint
panels.description: Round-trip only, deliberately excluding the limiter wait below it, so 'is Box slow' and 'are we throttling ourselves' stay separable. For file_content this is time-to-first-byte, NOT the download — that leg is box_content_transfer_duration_seconds, and reading it as the download is wrong by orders of magnitude.

panels.title: Rate Limiter Wait — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Sub-second is the interesting range; the ladder starts at 1ms.

panels.title: Augmenter Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: sent_without_acl is degraded success, not failure: when ListFileCollaborations fails the item is emitted anyway (stale metadata beats no metadata). Counting it as plain success is what made the old board overstate data quality. outcome=missing is also counted by items_skipped_not_found_total for the same event — never sum the two.

panels.title: last_access Coverage
panels.description: hit / (hit + miss) answers how much of the last_access we emit is real rather than unknown. The events-loaded rate underneath is the denominator behind it: a hit rate falling while events stop loading is a stale store, not a data problem.

panels.title: Augment Batch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Carries no datasource_id on purpose: the observation is deferred at the top of AugmentScan and the id is only recovered further in, per access-id group. So this is the one augmenter panel the pipeline board cannot break down by datasource — it still filters by namespace and pod, which come from the scrape, not from the instrument.

panels.title: Upload Throughput
panels.description: Bytes content-service confirmed in its UploadResponse — what the far side acknowledged, not what Box declared.

panels.title: NATS — Fetch Backlog
panels.description: Bulk and interactive durables together.

panels.title: Content Fetches by error_code (rate, 5m)
panels.description: NONE is the success case. The NAK_* codes are infra failures before or after a wire reply, where no FetchErrorCode applies — counting them is what makes fetch_total equal the number of deliveries the handler processed, not just the ones that produced a terminal reply. Timeout and too-large are error_code values here rather than their own counters, so an alert can target any code without a new series.

panels.title: Transfer p95 by size_bucket

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, size_bucket) (rate(box_content_transfer_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.description: Answers 'is the latency per file or per byte?'. Because the size is known before the transfer starts (Content-Length), it works on the failure path too — flip success to false. The unknown bucket is Box omitting Content-Length, not a zero-byte file, which is why it is not grouped with the small ones.

panels.title: NATS — Content Consumer Backlog
panels.description: Two durables share the CONTENT_FETCH stream: content-fetch-box for the bulk lane and content-fetch-box-interactive for See-Content. Split by consumer_name so an interactive-only backlog is visible instead of averaged away.

panels.title: KEDA — Content Replicas: current vs desired vs max
KEDA — Content Trigger Signals
panels.description: Three of the content ScaledObject's four effective triggers, all against the bulk durable. pipeline-full is not rendered in dev.

panels.title: KEDA — interactive-wakeup signal vs threshold
panels.description: The fourth trigger, and the one the scanner does not have: it watches the See-Content durable so an interactive-only backlog still wakes the pod. Without it scale-to-zero would strand every See-Content request into a 504.

panels.title: Gone — seen in trash by the scan
panels.description: Already in Box's trash at the moment we listed its parent folder.

panels.title: Gone — deleted per the event stream
panels.description: An ITEM_TRASH or DELETE event resolved by an incremental run.

panels.title: Gone — 404 on augment re-fetch
panels.description: Discovered by an earlier scan, and Box answered 404 when the augmenter went back for it.

panels.title: Files Gone by stage (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Three series, never one number. The augment series is 1:1 with box_augmenter_items_skipped_not_found_total — the same event increments both, and that second counter exists only so alerts can suppress this expected signal separately. Graphing both would be the same thing counted twice.

panels.title: Files Gone % (augment)

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(max_over_time(box_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*", outcome="missing"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(box_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="default", pod=~".*"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1))

panels.description: Share of everything the augmenter touched that Box no longer had.

panels.title: Slot Requeues (5m)
panels.description: Folders re-published because their user was saturated. This is back-pressure working: a re-publish resets the delivery count, so waiting never walks a folder toward the DLQ. Non-zero is normal under load.

panels.title: DLQ Depth
panels.description: Messages the SDK gave up on and removed from the stream. For the scanner each one is a FOLDER plus every subtree it would have expanded — so this count does not measure the damage: one discarded message cost 7 files when it hit a leaf, and would have cost thousands near the root. Any non-zero value means a scan silently returned less than the tenant holds. The connector's own funnel cannot show this: items_sent still equals files_discovered. See PLAN-deferral-dlq.md.

panels.title: DLQ Depth over time
panels.description: A step up here marks the moment a scan started losing folders. It is the only external evidence: the connector reports zero failures throughout.

panels.title: Scanner Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: The discovered line is not part of the stack — it is the denominator the stack should add up to.

panels.title: Folders by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Every subfolder is forked as its own message. skipped_collab is the owner filter: a folder owned by another user, left for that user's own fork so it is enumerated exactly once.

panels.title: Discovery → Sent Conversion
panels.description: The ratio the three parallel throughput lines hide. Anything below 1 is loss, and the panel next to it says how much in absolute terms.

panels.title: Item Loss (discovered − sent)
panels.description: Absolute leak per second, per datasource. Not the same question as the conversion ratio: a 99% conversion on a huge tenant can leak more files than a 60% conversion on a tiny one.

panels.title: Users Skipped by Reason (rate, 5m)
panels.description: The loss the file funnel above cannot see: these users' files were never discovered in the first place, so they never entered the funnel.

panels.title: Folder Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: One BoxFolderWork message: one folder listing plus the publishes and upserts it produces. This is the connector's real unit of work — multiply its mean by a folder count to estimate a larger tenant.

panels.title: Mean Cost per Folder
panels.description: Multiply by a folder count to estimate a larger tenant. This is the prediction question — 'if this enterprise grew 10x, how much folder work is that?' — and it is the reason the histogram is per-folder rather than per-scan.

panels.title: Scan Durations — three different units
panels.description: fan-out = authenticate + paged GET /users + publish one box.fork per user; EXCLUDES the traversal, which happens in other messages on other pods. incremental = a whole run including its inline augment. root_folder = one BoxFork, a user's root level only, not their tree. If fan-out and folder p95 come out similar, something is measuring what it does not think it is.

panels.title: Incremental Changes by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: outcome=deleted is Box's cleanest Files Gone signal: an explicit ITEM_TRASH/DELETE event, not a NOT_FOUND inferred after the fact. delete_failed is the one that used to surface only as a publishError to Observer.

panels.title: Incremental Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Unlike the fan-out, this really is the whole unit of work: events read, dedupe, deletes and the inline augment.

panels.title: Incremental Bailouts (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Runs that promoted themselves to a full scan because the change volume exceeded BOX_INCREMENTAL_MAX_RATIO of the known file count. Expensive, and until now visible only in the logs.

panels.title: Folder Work In-Flight & User Slots Held
panels.description: Both gauges are per pod and unlabeled by tenant — the slot scope is (datasource_access_id, user_id) while the deferral counter beside it is keyed by datasource_id, and minting a second label universe that cannot be joined to the first is the mistake to avoid. Flat at zero with the pods asleep is normal; flat WITH load would mean only one of the two folder entry points is instrumented.

panels.title: Slot Contention by Datasource (rate, 5m)
panels.description:
Two paths out of a saturated user, and the pair is the diagnostic:

requeues up, deferrals at zero — healthy. Folders that find no slot are re-published with their delivery count reset, so contention never walks them toward a discard.

deferrals above zero — folders are exhausting BOX_USER_SLOT_MAX_REQUEUE and falling back to a NAK. That spends a delivery, and past JOBENGINE_MAX_DELIVER the SDK removes the folder and everything below it. This is the last warning before silent loss.

both at zero — no contention; the user's slots are keeping up.

panels.title: Augmenter Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Exactly one outcome fires per item, so the stack sums to the batch size and this funnel checks itself the same way the scanner's does. sent_without_acl is degraded success — the item is emitted with no collaborations because ListFileCollaborations failed, on the principle that stale metadata beats no metadata. It is also the ACL-failure count; there is no separate acl_failures series, because the failure and the degraded emission are the same event.

panels.title: last_access Result (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Coverage of the events-derived last_access lookup. As a ratio it answers how much of the last_access we emit is real rather than unknown.

panels.title: Events Loaded into the Store (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Access events folded into the LastAccessStore on a refresh — the denominator behind the hit rate. A hit rate falling while this goes to zero is a stale store, not a data problem.

panels.title: Augment Batch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: The one augmenter panel that cannot be broken down by datasource: the observation is deferred at the top of AugmentScan and the id is only recovered further in, per access-id group. It still filters by pod, which comes from the scrape rather than the instrument — hence the missing .* here is deliberate, not an oversight.

panels.title: Skipped Not-Found (rate, 5m)
panels.description: 1:1 with items_processed_total{outcome="missing"} — the same event increments both. It exists so alerts can suppress this expected signal independently. Graphed alone here, and never added to the outcome panel: that would be the same thing counted twice.

panels.title: Content Fetches by error_code (rate, 5m)
panels.description: NONE is success. Timeout and too-large are error_code values rather than their own counters, which is what lets an alert target any code without adding a series. The NAK_* codes are infra failures before or after a wire reply — counting them is what makes fetch_total equal the deliveries the handler processed.

panels.title: Transfer p95 by size_bucket — success

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, size_bucket) (rate(box_content_transfer_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.description: 'Is the latency per file or per byte?' — the size_bucket label answers it directly. Buckets are cut at 1 MiB / 10 MiB / 100 MiB.

panels.title: Transfer p95 by size_bucket — failure

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, size_bucket) (rate(box_content_transfer_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="false"}[5m])))

panels.description: Half the value of the size_bucket label: the size is known from Content-Length before the transfer starts, so it works on the failure path too. An 80MiB file that dies halfway through the upload and a 2KiB file that fails to open are two different incidents; without this they are one series.

panels.title: Content Fetch Duration — p50 / p95 / p99

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(box_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(box_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(box_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.description: End-to-end handler latency. Success and failure are separate label values so a slow-failing request does not poison the success p99.

panels.title: Content Fetch Bytes — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Size distribution of successfully streamed files, 1KiB to ~1GiB. Unlabeled by tenant, so this one is not filtered by .*.

panels.title: Uploaded Bytes (rate)
panels.description: Bytes content-service confirmed in its UploadResponse — what the far side acknowledged, not what Box declared.

panels.title: Content Fetch p95 by access_id

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, datasource_access_id) (rate(box_content_fetch_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="default", pod=~".*", datasource_access_id=~".*", success="true"}[5m])))

panels.description: Which tenant is slow. 'unknown' here means the failure happened before the URN could be parsed.

panels.title: Fetch Errors by error_code (increase, 1h)
panels.description: Triage table: non-NONE error codes over the last hour. NAK_* are infra-level failures on the NATS path, not Box refusing us.

panels.title: Content Requests In-Flight
panels.description: Content mode's saturation signal, the counterpart of the scanner's folder_work_in_flight. Per pod and unlabeled by tenant.

panels.title: Average Bytes per Fetch
panels.description: An average of averages, not a distribution: one 1GB file and a thousand 1KB files land on the same point as a thousand medium ones. The size_bucket panels above are the real answer; this is the cheap sanity check next to them.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: Container series carry no job label, so these two select on the pod name instead of ${box_component}. The pattern covers both deployments — box-connector-be-go and box-connector-be-go-content.

panels.title: GC Pause — max & median
panels.description: go_gc_duration_seconds is a SUMMARY, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series and histogram_quantile over it returns nothing. Available quantiles are 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 — there is no 0.99.

panels.title: Graph 429 rate (RATE_LIMITED)
panels.description:
Non-zero here means Microsoft Graph is throttling our app registration. This is the metric the whole NXE-2480 hypothesis turns on.

NOTE: if the connector cannot read the HTTP status it falls through to CONNECTION_FAILED instead, so check the breakdown panel too rather than reading a zero here as proof.

panels.title: Fetch errors by code
panels.description:
FetchErrorCode as classified by classifyGraphError (internal/fetch/handler.go:339).

RETRYABLE (these are the dangerous ones — content-service will retry each 15x): RATE_LIMITED, CONNECTION_FAILED, TIMEOUT, READ_ERROR, CACHE_WRITE_FAILED
NON-RETRYABLE (cheap, fail once): NOT_FOUND, PERMISSION_DENIED, INVALID_URN, TOO_LARGE, INTERNAL(4xx)

panels.title: Fetch failure fraction
panels.description: errors / (errors + successes). A few percent is normal — deleted files and permission denials. What matters is whether those failures are RETRYABLE, which the panel to the left answers.

panels.title: Fetch outcomes
panels.description: Success, error, timeout and too-large rates side by side. TIMEOUT and TOO_LARGE have their own counters and do NOT appear in sharepoint_content_fetch_error_total.

panels.title: Fetch duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: End-to-end duration of one ContentFetchRequest inside the connector. Compare against content-service's content_nats_worker_duration_seconds — they measure nearly the same span from opposite ends, and a divergence means time is being spent in the NATS hop.

panels.title: Graph request rate
panels.description:
Requests leaving the connector toward graph.microsoft.com.

During a retry storm this should show the amplification directly: content-service retries each failed document up to 15 times, and every one of those attempts becomes a fresh Graph call.

panels.title: Graph 5xx rate  (NOTE: EXCLUDES 429)
panels.description: Server errors only. THROTTLING IS 429 AND IS NOT COUNTED HERE. Do not read a flat line as 'Graph was healthy' — see the reference panel at the bottom of this dashboard.

panels.title: Graph request duration p95
panels.description: Measured by the connector's TelemetryMiddleware around the whole round trip, including the 302 redirect to the CDN host.

panels.title: Billed spend (range)
panels.description: assignSensitivityLabel is the only metered call in Microsoft Graph, at $0.00185 USD each. This is billed calls over the selected time range × that unit price — the real invoice line, not an estimate from outcome arithmetic.

panels.title: Billed calls (range)
panels.description: Writes actually issued to Graph. Every other outcome is free. A run whose billed count is close to its item count means almost nothing was already correct — check the mapping before repeating it.

panels.title: Applied (range)
panels.description: Label written and the Graph operation reached a terminal success state. This is the only outcome that changed a document.

panels.title: Skipped — already correct (range)
panels.description: The file already carried the target label, so no Graph call was made and nothing was billed. On a re-run of an unchanged corpus this should dominate; if it is near zero on a second pass, the apply is not sticking.

panels.title: Terminal rejections (range)
panels.description: Outcomes that will never succeed on retry: label_missing (an admin deleted it — the MAPPING is stale), unsupported_label, not_appliable (the target is a label group), file_locked (423 on a file SharePoint cannot decrypt), and failed. Non-zero means someone has to change something; re-running only costs money.

panels.title: Pending unterminated (range)
panels.description: Graph accepted the write but the operation had not reached a terminal state before the poll window closed. NOT a failure — the apply may still land, and it was already billed. Re-issuing would double-bill and may double-apply, so treat a rising count as a reason to widen LABELSYNC_POLL_WINDOW, never as a reason to retry.

panels.title: Label-sync outcomes
panels.description: Every document the label-sync handler resolved, by outcome. Stacked, so the total height is throughput. The split between the free outcomes (skipped_already_correct, the pre-flight rejections) and the billed one (applied) is the cost story.

panels.title: Billed call rate and cost per hour
panels.description: Left axis is calls/sec; the second series projects the current rate to USD/hour at $0.00185 per call. Use it to sanity-check a large run before it finishes rather than after the invoice.

panels.title: Terminal rejections — something has to change
panels.description: None of these get better by retrying. label_missing and unsupported_label point at the mapping; not_appliable means the mapped target is a label GROUP rather than a label; file_locked is about the document itself (double-key encrypted, or protected in a way SharePoint cannot decrypt).

panels.title: Transient — worth another run
panels.description: deferred_retry_later is 423 fileDecryptionDeferred: the service is saying it can do this, just not now. deferred_label_pending means the mapped label was not in the tenant at write time but the registry saw it live recently, so this is propagation rather than deletion. rejected_label_disabled may reverse when an admin turns the label back on.

panels.title: Billed writes that did not resolve
panels.description: pending_unterminated against the billed-call rate. The gap is money spent on writes whose outcome we never observed. A persistent gap means the poll window is too short for this tenant, not that the writes failed.

options.content:
**Label sync runs in SCANNER mode only.** Set **Component = Scanner** (or leave it on All) — the `.*` and `.*` variables on the rest of this dashboard are driven by `sharepoint_content_fetch_*`, which only the *content* pod emits, so they can never name the pod doing this work. That is why this row selects on `${sharepoint_component}` instead.

**Blank panels are the expected state until the feature is switched on**, and they are the *only* outward signal that it is not. The producer half is gated behind `LABELSYNC_PRODUCER_ENABLED`, which defaults to false; left unset, a label-sync job finds no handler and vanishes with no error, no log line and no failed job. In Kubernetes the switch is the Helm value `sharepointConnectorBeGo.labelSync.producerEnabled` on the **scanner** deployment — content mode never registers the handlers. Check it before assuming the pipeline is broken:

```
kubectl get cm -o jsonpath='{.data.LABELSYNC_PRODUCER_ENABLED}' \
  <release>-applications-sharepoint-connector-be-go-config
```

**Only `applied` costs money.** `skipped_already_correct` and the pre-flight rejections are free; `assignSensitivityLabel` is the one metered call in Graph, at **$0.00185** each. An `_cached` suffix on an outcome means the verdict came from the label cache rather than a fresh read — same meaning, no Graph call.

**429s do not appear here.** Graph throttling shows up in the Throttling row at the top of this dashboard, and only for content mode. Scanner-side Graph traffic is on the *Microsoft Graph API* row, gated by `.*`.

panels.title: Graph client in-flight by app registration
panels.description:
SHAPE MATTERS MORE THAN VALUE.

sawtooth returning to 0 between scans -> healthy
monotonic ratchet never returning to 0 -> the Redis in-flight counter is leaking, and the connector will start blocking on every fetch once all clients exceed maxInflight

See the panel to the right for the two-minute test that settles it.

options.content:
## In-flight leak — the rival explanation

The connector picks a Graph **app registration** by fewest in-flight requests, counted in **Redis**: `Incr()` before each call, `Decr()` after (`graphhelper.go:122-137`). Any request that dies in between leaks a count **permanently** — the 15-minute `Expire` is refreshed on every `Incr`, so it never fires under sustained load.

Once every client exceeds `maxInflight`, `getClient()` **blocks on every fetch** (`graphhelper.go:326-358`) — and that code path has **no log statement at all**, so it leaves no trace.

### Reading the panel to the left
* **sawtooth returning to 0 between scans** -> healthy
* **monotonic ratchet that never returns to 0** -> leaking

### The decisive test (2 minutes, no history needed)
```
# with the connector IDLE:
KEYS  inflight:*
GET   inflight:<clientID>    # per Graph app registration
```
Every value **must** be 0 on an idle connector. Any non-zero value is a leak. Stronger: restart the pod, wait for idle, re-read — the counters live in Redis, not the pod, so a restart does not clear them.

### Telling the two apart
**Throttling** -> `"graph DownloadDriveItem failed"` lines with `http_status` 429.
**Leak** -> slow fetches with **no error lines at all**.

panels.title: Container restarts
panels.description: The SharePoint content connector runs at replicaCount: 1. A restart mid-scan drops every in-flight fetch, and — because the in-flight counters live in Redis rather than in the pod — leaks them.

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description: Time the container spent throttled against its CFS quota. A single replica serving the whole bulk content path will show up here before it shows up anywhere else.

panels.title: Memory working set
panels.description: Downloads are streamed, so this should stay flat regardless of file size. A climb that tracks scan volume means something is buffering whole files.

panels.title: What this dashboard can and cannot tell you

options.content:
## Read this before trusting a flat graph

### There is no 429 counter in the `graph_*` family
`graph_requests_5xx` counts **only** 5xx. Microsoft Graph throttling arrives as **HTTP 429**, which is 4xx, and **nothing counts it**.

A flat `graph_requests_5xx` does **not** mean Graph was healthy.

Throttling is visible in exactly two places:
1. `sharepoint_content_fetch_error_total{code="FETCH_ERROR_RATE_LIMITED"}` — the panels above
2. the connector logs — grep `"graph DownloadDriveItem failed"`, logged at WARN with an `http_status` field

### The error body is thrown away
`internal/graphhelper/download.go:101-106` drains and **discards** the Graph error body, and never reads `Retry-After`. So we can see *that* we were throttled but not the Graph error code (`activityLimitReached`) nor how long Microsoft asked us to wait.

### Why one connector's problem kills a privacy scan
content-service does not enumerate `FETCH_ERROR_RATE_LIMITED` in `mapFetchError`, so it falls to the `default` branch and is treated as **retryable** — 5 in-process attempts with 1/2/4/8s backoff, then Nak'd for up to 3 JetStream deliveries. **15 calls to Graph per document**, with Graph's own `Retry-After` ignored. Retrying a throttle deepens it.
